title: From Eight Michelin Stars to Your Pantry: Gymkhana Brings Indian Sauces to Whole Foods
excerpt: The London-based restaurant empire behind 30 concepts and eight Michelin stars is betting that Americans are ready to cook restaurant-quality Indian food at home.
body:
For most NRIs, the name Gymkhana conjures memories of colonial-era social clubs — grand establishments where India's elite once gathered over billiards and whisky. For the Sethi siblings of London, it became the name of a Michelin-starred restaurant that helped redefine Indian fine dining in the West. Now, the family behind one of Britain's most celebrated restaurant groups is attempting something far more ambitious: putting those same flavors on every grocery shelf in America.

Gymkhana Fine Foods, a new line of simmer sauces, marinades, and chutneys developed by JKS Restaurants, has launched exclusively at Whole Foods Markets nationwide. The move, announced this week alongside an $8.5 million Series A funding round led by CAVU Consumer Partners, marks one of the most significant entries of a high-end Indian restaurant brand into the American consumer-packaged goods market.

## Restaurant Pedigree, Retail Ambition

JKS Restaurants, founded by siblings Jyotin, Karam, and Sunaina Sethi, operates more than 30 concepts across the UK. The portfolio — which includes Trishna, Brigadiers, BiBi, and the Punjabi-focused Ambassadors Clubhouse in New York — boasts a collective eight Michelin stars and six Bib Gourmand mentions, a record that places JKS among the most decorated Indian restaurant groups in the world.

The Gymkhana restaurant itself, which opened on Albemarle Street in London's Mayfair in 2013, earned its first Michelin star within six months. Last year, JKS made its U.S. restaurant debut with Gymkhana at the Aria Resort & Casino in Las Vegas, bringing its signature blend of Mughlai-inspired grills and seasonal Indian cooking to the Strip.

"Each sauce, marinade and chutney has been created to deliver the same bold, authentic flavors found in our restaurants," Karam Sethi, culinary and creative director for JKS, said in a statement. "As we expand into the U.S., from our first restaurant in Las Vegas in 2025 to the launch of Gymkhana Fine Foods across the country, our aim remains the same: to offer Indian cuisine in its purest form, whether you're cooking in your own kitchen or dining with us."

## The Money Behind the Mission

The $8.5 million funding round is led by CAVU Consumer Partners, co-founded by Rohan Oza — the Indian-born investor best known for his appearances on ABC's *Shark Tank* and his track record of building brands like Vitaminwater and Bai. Oza's involvement sends a signal: this is not a vanity project from a restaurant group dabbling in retail. It is a properly capitalized bet on Indian food's next frontier.

The CPG line is co-founded by Gulrez Arora, who helped grow the retail products in the UK before crossing the Atlantic. The Whole Foods exclusive gives the brand premium shelf positioning, placing Gymkhana's products alongside the organic tahinis and artisan pasta sauces that dominate the natural foods aisle.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For the 5.1 million Indians living in the United States, the launch addresses a quiet frustration: the gap between what you can eat at a great Indian restaurant and what you can realistically cook on a Tuesday night. Jarred Indian sauces have long been available in American grocery stores, but most cater to a non-Indian palate — heavy on sugar, light on complexity, with labels that treat "curry" as a single monolithic flavor.

Gymkhana's entry, backed by genuine culinary authority, represents a different proposition. These are products developed by chefs who have spent a decade earning Michelin stars for their mastery of regional Indian cooking — from the charcoal-kissed kebabs of Lucknow to the coconut-laced curries of Kerala.

The timing aligns with a broader surge in Indian food's presence in the American market. Indian restaurants in the US now number over 40,000, part of a $15 billion market that is growing faster than any other ethnic cuisine category. The U.S. imported $711 million worth of Indian spices in 2024-25, up from $619 million the previous year. Haldiram's generates 40 percent of its export revenue from the US via Amazon.

## What's Next

The Whole Foods launch is just the beginning. JKS has signaled plans to expand Gymkhana Fine Foods beyond its initial exclusive retail partner, and the restaurant group itself continues to grow its American footprint. With Ambassadors Clubhouse already open in New York and the Las Vegas Gymkhana drawing steady crowds, the Sethi siblings are building an Indian food empire that stretches from white-tablecloth dining rooms to supermarket aisles.

For NRIs who have long wished they could bottle the magic of a great Gymkhana meal and take it home, that wish is now, quite literally, on the shelf.
